questions.question: What does a permission boundary do in AWS IAM?

options.text: It grants additional permissions beyond what identity policies allow
It sets the maximum permissions an identity-based policy can grant
It replaces identity-based policies entirely
It applies only during cross-account role assumptions

explanation.correct: A permission boundary sets the ceiling — the maximum permissions an IAM user or role can ever have. It never grants permissions on its own.
explanation.why: A is wrong — boundaries never open up permissions. C is wrong — identity policies still apply (intersection is used). D is wrong — boundaries apply across all sessions of the entity.

questions.question: A permission boundary contains only Deny statements. What is the effective result for the IAM user it is attached to?

options.text: The user can perform all actions allowed by their identity policy
The user can perform no actions at all
The Deny statements override all allows system-wide
The boundary is ignored because it has no Allow statements

explanation.correct: A boundary works by intersection of allows. If the boundary has no Allow statements, the allowed set is empty — so the intersection with any identity policy is also empty. The user can do nothing.
explanation.why: A is wrong — intersection collapses to empty. C is wrong — Deny statements in a boundary affect only that entity. D is wrong — the boundary is not ignored; it just results in no permissions.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes how effective permissions are calculated when both an identity-based policy and a permission boundary are present?

options.text: The union of both policies — all actions allowed by either
The identity policy takes precedence over the boundary
The intersection — only actions allowed by BOTH the identity policy and the boundary
The boundary takes precedence over the identity policy

explanation.correct: Effective permissions = intersection of identity policy and permission boundary. Only actions that both allow are effective.
explanation.why: A (union) would widen permissions, not cap them. B and D are both wrong — neither 'takes precedence'; the intersection is the rule.

questions.question: When does a session policy apply?

options.text: It is attached permanently to an IAM role
It is passed as a parameter at the time of calling STS AssumeRole
It applies across all sessions of the entity indefinitely
It is attached to the calling principal before role assumption

explanation.correct: A session policy is passed as a parameter when you call STS AssumeRole. It applies only to that one specific session — the role itself is not changed.
explanation.why: A describes identity-based policies or permission boundaries. C describes permission boundaries. D is incorrect — the calling principal's policies are dropped after assumption.

questions.question: A role's permission policy allows S3:GetObject and S3:PutObject. A session policy passed at assume time allows S3:GetObject and S3:DeleteObject. What can the resulting session do?

options.text: GetObject, PutObject, and DeleteObject
GetObject only
GetObject and DeleteObject
GetObject and PutObject

explanation.correct: Session effective permissions = intersection of role policy and session policy. Only S3:GetObject is in both, so that is the only allowed action.
explanation.why: A is union — wrong. C includes DeleteObject which the role doesn't allow. D includes PutObject which the session policy doesn't allow.

questions.question: A developer in Account B needs to access an S3 bucket in Account A using an IAM role. What TWO things are required for the cross-account role assumption to succeed?

options.text: The developer's user in Account B must have STS:AssumeRole permission, AND the role in Account A must have a trust policy naming Account B
The S3 bucket policy in Account A must explicitly allow Account B, AND Account B must have a service control policy allowing S3 access
AWS Organizations must be configured, AND a VPC peering connection must exist between accounts
The developer must have an IAM user in Account A, AND the S3 bucket must be public

explanation.correct: Cross-account access is a two-policy handshake: (1) the caller in Account B needs STS:AssumeRole permission, and (2) the role in Account A needs a trust policy that names Account B as a trusted principal.
explanation.why: B is not the standard pattern for role-based access. C is wrong — Organizations and VPC peering are not required. D violates least-privilege and long-lived credential security requirements.

questions.question: After a principal in Account B successfully assumes a role in Account A, which policies govern the session?

options.text: The principal's identity policies in Account B plus the role's permission policy in Account A
The role's permission policy and the role's own permission boundary in Account A
The principal's permission boundary in Account B plus the role's trust policy in Account A
All policies in both Account A and Account B are evaluated together

explanation.correct: Once role assumption succeeds, the session is governed exclusively by the role's permission policy and the role's own boundary. The assuming principal's identity policies and permission boundaries are dropped.
explanation.why: A is wrong — the caller's identity policies are set aside after assumption. C is wrong — the caller's boundary does not follow into the assumed session. D is wrong — AWS does not combine all policies across accounts.

questions.question: You want to ensure that developers who assume the 'ReadOnlyAnalyst' role can never exceed read-only access, regardless of which developer assumes it. What is the correct control?

options.text: Attach a permission boundary to each developer's IAM user that restricts them to read-only
Attach a permission boundary to the ReadOnlyAnalyst role itself
Add a Deny policy to each developer's identity policy
Use a service control policy in the developer's organizational unit

explanation.correct: The boundary must be on the role, not the user. The user's boundary is not evaluated for the assumed session. Putting the boundary on the role caps every session regardless of who assumes it.
explanation.why: A is the classic trap — user boundaries are dropped at assumption time. C is hard to manage at scale and doesn't persist into role sessions. D uses SCPs which operate at the account level, not per-role.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the External ID condition in a trust policy for third-party cross-account access?

options.text: It limits the session duration of role assumptions
It prevents the Confused Deputy problem by requiring a unique per-customer identifier on every AssumeRole call
It restricts role assumption to specific IP addresses
It replaces the need for a permission boundary on the role

explanation.correct: External ID is the AWS-documented mechanism for preventing the Confused Deputy problem. A SaaS vendor generates a unique value per customer; the customer requires that exact value in the trust policy. Even if a different customer learns the role ARN, the assumption fails without the correct External ID.
explanation.why: A describes duration_seconds. C describes aws:SourceIp condition, which does not solve Confused Deputy. D is wrong — External ID handles identity confusion, not permission scoping.

questions.question: A SaaS vendor needs to scope each role assumption to a specific S3 prefix per customer, even though the role's permission policy is broader. What mechanism accomplishes this?

options.text: Attach a permission boundary to the vendor's IAM user
Set duration_seconds to 900 so the session expires quickly
Pass a session policy as a parameter to STS:AssumeRole that limits access to the specific bucket and prefix
Attach a resource-based policy to the S3 bucket for each customer's role

explanation.correct: A session policy passed at AssumeRole time scopes just that one assumption. The resulting session's effective permissions = intersection of the role's policy and the session policy — capped to exactly the specified prefix.
explanation.why: A — vendor user boundary is dropped at assumption. B — short duration limits credential lifetime but doesn't prevent wrong-customer access. D — resource policies don't deliver per-assumption scoping.

questions.question: What is the difference between aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent and aws:MultiFactorAuthAge?

options.text: MultiFactorAuthPresent is a numeric value; MultiFactorAuthAge is a boolean
MultiFactorAuthPresent is true for the entire session lifetime; MultiFactorAuthAge measures seconds since MFA was used
MultiFactorAuthPresent expires after 15 minutes; MultiFactorAuthAge persists the whole session
Both are the same — they are aliases for the same condition key

explanation.correct: MultiFactorAuthPresent is a boolean that is set at session start and remains true for the entire session lifetime. MultiFactorAuthAge is a numeric value (seconds) that increases as the session ages — used to enforce fresh MFA for sensitive operations.
explanation.why: A has them backwards. C has them backwards. D is wrong — they serve completely different purposes.

questions.question: Which condition key should you use to protect against session hijacking on destructive operations like S3:DeleteObject?

options.text: aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent
aws:SecureTransport
aws:MultiFactorAuthAge with a threshold like 900
aws:RequestedRegion

explanation.correct: aws:MultiFactorAuthAge with a small threshold (e.g., 900 seconds = 15 minutes) requires the user to have performed MFA recently. A hijacked session loses this condition as time passes, blocking destructive actions.
explanation.why: A (MultiFactorAuthPresent) stays true for the whole session — a hijacked session retains it. B enforces HTTPS but not MFA. D restricts by region, not by MFA recency.

questions.question: A cross-account call to a KMS-encrypted S3 bucket in Account A from an EC2 instance in Account B fails with Access Denied. Which FOUR places should you check in order?

options.text: Principal's IAM policy in Account B, role trust policy in Account A, bucket policy in Account A, KMS key policy in Account A
Bucket policy in Account A, KMS key policy in Account A, VPC route tables, security groups
Account B's SCPs, Account A's SCPs, the bucket ACL, the KMS key rotation settings
CloudTrail logs in Account B, IAM Access Analyzer in Account A, bucket versioning, encryption settings

explanation.correct: The four places are: (1) principal's IAM policy in the source account (Account B), (2) role trust policy in the destination account (Account A), (3) bucket policy in Account A, (4) KMS key policy in Account A. Both the IAM role policy AND the KMS key policy must independently permit KMS:Decrypt.
explanation.why: B misses the source account IAM policy check. C and D check wrong things — SCPs, ACLs, rotation, and CloudTrail are not the authorization chain.

questions.question: In a cross-account scenario where EC2 in Account B accesses S3 in Account A, which account is the SOURCE account?

options.text: Account A — because that is where the S3 bucket lives
Account B — because that is where the call originates from
Whichever account has the trust policy
The AWS Management Account in the organization

explanation.correct: The source account is where the call originates — Account B (where EC2 is). The destination account is Account A (where S3 and the KMS key are). The caller needs STS:AssumeRole permission in the source account; the role's trust policy is in the destination account.
explanation.why: A is the destination, not source. C is the destination account by definition. D has no bearing on source/destination.

questions.question: Which IAM policy type is attached to AWS resources (like S3 buckets, KMS keys, Lambda) rather than to IAM identities?

options.text: Identity-based policy
Permission boundary
Resource-based policy
Session policy

explanation.correct: Resource-based policies are attached to AWS resources and answer 'who can do what to this resource?' The Principal element is explicit in these policies.
explanation.why: A attaches to IAM identities (users, groups, roles). B is an advanced IAM feature attached to identities as a cap. D is passed at AssumeRole time, not attached to anything permanently.

questions.question: Which of the following services support resource-based policies? (Select the most complete correct list)

options.text: EC2, ECS, Auto Scaling, CloudFormation
S3, KMS, SQS, SNS, Lambda, ECR, EFS, API Gateway, Secrets Manager
All AWS services support resource-based policies
Only S3 supports resource-based policies

explanation.correct: The services that support resource-based policies are: S3, KMS, SQS, SNS, Lambda, ECR, EFS, API Gateway, and Secrets Manager. All other services rely on identity-based policies only.
explanation.why: A lists compute/infra services that do NOT support resource-based policies. C is incorrect — most services rely on identity-based policies only. D severely understates the list.

questions.question: An explicit deny in a bucket policy applies to which principals?

options.text: Only principals without an identity-based Allow for the action
Only cross-account principals
All principals, including those whose identity-based policies would otherwise allow the action
Only the root user of the account

explanation.correct: An explicit deny in a resource-based policy (like a bucket policy) overrides any allow — from identity-based policies, permission boundaries, or session policies. This is the invariant AWS IAM rule: explicit deny wins everywhere.
explanation.why: A is wrong — explicit deny wins over allows. B is wrong — it applies same-account and cross-account. D is wrong — it applies to all principals named in the deny.

questions.question: IAM groups cannot be referenced as Principals in which type of policy?

options.text: Identity-based policies
Resource-based policies
Permission boundaries
Service Control Policies

explanation.correct: IAM groups cannot be principals in resource-based policies. Groups are containers for permission management, not identities. When writing bucket policies or KMS key policies, you must reference the underlying users or roles, not the groups.
explanation.why: Identity-based policies do attach to groups (to all members). Permission boundaries and SCPs are not resource-attached policies where Principal matters in the same way.

questions.question: What are the three steps in IAM's policy evaluation order?

options.text: Explicit Allow → Explicit Deny → Implicit Deny
Implicit Deny → Explicit Allow → Explicit Deny
Explicit Deny → Explicit Allow → Implicit Deny
Explicit Allow → Implicit Deny → Explicit Deny

explanation.correct: AWS IAM always evaluates in this order: (1) Explicit Deny — if found anywhere, stop and deny. (2) Explicit Allow — if found and no deny, allow. (3) Implicit Deny — if neither deny nor allow, deny by default. AWS is deny-by-default.
explanation.why: All other orderings are wrong. Explicit Deny must be checked first and always wins.

questions.question: A developer has an identity-based policy granting S3:DeleteObject on a bucket. The bucket has a bucket policy with an explicit deny for S3:DeleteObject for all principals except the backup role. The developer is NOT the backup role. What happens when the developer calls S3:DeleteObject?

options.text: The call succeeds because the identity-based allow takes precedence over the bucket policy deny
The call is denied because the bucket policy's explicit deny overrides the identity-based allow
The call succeeds because identity-based and resource-based policies are evaluated independently
The call succeeds because same-account identity-based allows always win over resource-based denies

explanation.correct: Explicit deny anywhere wins. The bucket policy's explicit deny applies to all principals except the backup role. The developer's identity-based allow is overridden by this explicit deny. The IAM evaluation rule is invariant.
explanation.why: A, C, D all contradict the fundamental IAM rule: explicit deny overrides any allow, in any policy type, same account or cross-account.

questions.question: Which AWS service issues the temporary credentials (access key ID, secret access key, session token) used during role assumption?

options.text: AWS IAM
AWS KMS
AWS Security Token Service (STS)
AWS Secrets Manager

explanation.correct: AWS Security Token Service (STS) issues temporary credentials when a role is assumed. These include an access key ID, secret access key, and session token — all of which expire when the session ends.
explanation.why: IAM manages long-lived identity and policy definitions, not temporary credentials. KMS handles encryption keys. Secrets Manager stores secrets — it does not issue session tokens.

questions.question: How does AWS IAM handle authorization once a principal from Account B has successfully assumed a role in Account A?

options.text: The session uses Account B's policies plus Account A's role policies
AWS treats it as a same-account call made by the assumed role identity in Account A
Both accounts' SCPs are evaluated together for every API call
The session reverts to Account B's principal after each API call

explanation.correct: Once the role is assumed, from IAM's perspective the session is local to Account A — it is a same-account call made by the assumed role identity. The cross-account aspect is resolved at assumption time, not per-call.
explanation.why: A is wrong — Account B's policies are dropped. C is wrong — SCPs from Account B don't continue to apply. D is wrong — the session persists as the role identity.

questions.question: Which MFA mechanism is considered phishing-resistant and binds credentials to the original domain?

options.text: Virtual MFA (TOTP app like Google Authenticator)
Hardware MFA token (time-based physical device)
FIDO security key (e.g., Google Titan, YubiKey)
SMS MFA

explanation.correct: FIDO security keys use public key cryptography and are phishing-resistant. The credential is bound to the original domain and cannot be replayed against a different domain — making them ideal for privileged identities like root users.
explanation.why: Virtual MFA (TOTP) is not phishing-resistant. Hardware MFA tokens share the same phishing weakness as virtual. SMS MFA was deprecated in 2019 and is the least secure.

questions.question: SMS MFA is deprecated in AWS IAM since which year?

explanation.correct: SMS MFA was deprecated in 2019. Existing configurations remain functional but new ones cannot be created, and AWS enforces migration away from SMS in production environments.
explanation.why: The other years are incorrect. This is a commonly tested IAM exam fact.

questions.question: A security scenario requires ensuring that MFA was performed within the last 15 minutes before any S3:DeleteObject call succeeds. Which condition key and comparison should you use?

options.text: aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent: true
aws:MultiFactorAuthAge with NumericLessThan: 900
aws:MultiFactorAuthAge with NumericGreaterThan: 900
aws:TokenIssueTime with DateLessThan: now-15min

explanation.correct: aws:MultiFactorAuthAge returns seconds since MFA was issued. NumericLessThan 900 means 'MFA was done less than 900 seconds (15 minutes) ago.' This enforces freshness and protects against hijacked sessions.
explanation.why: A (Present) stays true for the whole session — no freshness guarantee. C (NumericGreaterThan 900) would ALLOW old MFA, the opposite of what you want. D is not a valid IAM condition key.

questions.question: A company wants read operations to succeed all day after morning sign-in with MFA, but requires fresh MFA for any deletion. What is the correct IAM architecture?

options.text: Apply aws:MultiFactorAuthAge: 900 to ALL operations
Apply aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent: true to read operations; apply aws:MultiFactorAuthAge: 900 to delete operations
Apply aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent: true to delete operations; apply aws:MultiFactorAuthAge: 900 to read operations
Disable MFA for read operations entirely; use MFA only for writes

explanation.correct: The production pattern is: MultiFactorAuthPresent (boolean, session-wide) for read-only operations — the session MFA at sign-in is sufficient. MultiFactorAuthAge with small threshold for destructive operations — requires fresh MFA. This balances usability with security.
explanation.why: A requires fresh MFA for reads too — poor UX. C reverses the logic — age-gating reads is overly restrictive. D removes security entirely for reads.

questions.question: A permission boundary is attached to a user. The user assumes a role. Does the user's permission boundary apply during the role session?

options.text: Yes — the user's boundary follows them into every session they create
Yes — but only if the role is in the same AWS account
No — the user's boundary applies only when the user acts with its own identity, not during assumed role sessions
No — permission boundaries never apply to users, only roles

explanation.correct: A user's permission boundary applies only to that user's direct actions with its own identity. When the user assumes a role, the user's boundary is not evaluated. The session is governed by the role's policies and the role's own boundary. This is the most commonly missed IAM fact on the SAA exam.
explanation.why: A is the trap answer — it incorrectly assumes the boundary follows the user. B is also wrong. D is wrong — permission boundaries do apply to users for their direct actions.

questions.question: Which of the following is the correct mental model for the four IAM security mechanisms?

options.text: Identity policies = ceiling; Boundaries = floor; Resource policies = gate; Conditions = key
Identity policies = floor (grant baseline); Boundaries = ceiling (cap max); Resource policies = gate (absolute deny + cross-account); Conditions = contextual gates
Boundaries = grant permissions; Identity policies = restrict permissions; Resource policies = audit; Conditions = logging
All four mechanisms work identically — they are just applied at different scopes

explanation.correct: The four mechanisms: Identity policies = floor (grants baseline), Permission boundaries = ceiling (caps max), Resource policies = gate (absolute deny that no identity allow can override; enables cross-account), Condition keys = contextual gates (source IP, MFA, time, tags, region).
explanation.why: A reverses floor and ceiling. C is completely wrong — boundaries never grant. D is wrong — each mechanism has a distinct role and evaluation behavior.

questions.question: A SaaS vendor uses a single IAM role per customer account. To prevent customer A's data from being accessed while serving customer B, and to scope each session to a specific S3 prefix, which TWO mechanisms are needed?

options.text: STS External ID in the trust policy + Session policy passed at AssumeRole time
IP address restriction in the trust policy + Short session duration (900 seconds)
Permission boundary on the role + CloudTrail logging
S3 bucket policy deny + KMS key policy restriction

explanation.correct: External ID prevents Confused Deputy (identity confusion between customers). Session policy scopes each assumption to the per-customer prefix. These two mechanisms together satisfy both requirements: correct-customer identity guarantee and per-call permission scoping.
explanation.why: B — IP restriction doesn't prevent Confused Deputy; short duration doesn't prevent wrong-customer access. C — permission boundary applies across all sessions, can't do per-call scoping. D — bucket/KMS policies are static, not per-assumption.

questions.question: When a cross-account call to a KMS-encrypted S3 bucket fails with Access Denied, and you confirm the principal's IAM policy in the source account is correct, which TWO things in the destination account must BOTH allow KMS:Decrypt?

options.text: The S3 bucket ACL and the KMS key rotation policy
The IAM role's permission policy AND the KMS key's resource policy
The trust policy and the service control policy
The CloudTrail event policy and the IAM role boundary

explanation.correct: KMS uses two-pronged authorization: BOTH the IAM role's permission policy AND the KMS key's resource policy must independently permit KMS:Decrypt. This applies in same-account scenarios too, but cross-account makes it more visible. Exam answers that mention only one of the two are distractors.
explanation.why: A — ACLs and rotation policies don't govern access. C — trust policy handles who can assume the role, not what it can decrypt. D — CloudTrail is for auditing, not authorization.
